content:
The Chinese woman at the centre of the scandal that cost Jensen Huang his job at Nvidia stayed in contact with an officer of China's top intelligence agency for more than a year, including throughout her secret affair with the chipmaker's then chief executive, according to a report in The New York Times on Sunday. The contacts ran from the spring of 2025 until the autumn of this year, the newspaper said, citing multiple people with knowledge of American intelligence reports that describe the encounters.

Alice Huang's contacts with the Ministry of State Security overlapped not only with her relationship with Huang, but also with a period when her company, Megaspeed, was buying large quantities of advanced Nvidia chips. Some of those chips went to data centres in South-East Asia serving Chinese technology companies such as Alibaba, according to the report, while others are suspected of having been smuggled into China in breach of American export controls. The intelligence gathered by the United States includes evidence, including shipping records, showing the roles played by Huang and her business partner in that network of companies, the people familiar with the reports said.

That business partner, Kang Wei, who was often introduced to associates as her husband, also worked with the same Chinese intelligence agency, according to the people with knowledge of the intelligence. The extent and precise timing of Huang's contacts with the agency, and of Kang's work for it, had not previously been reported. Megaspeed said earlier this month that Alice Huang had officially left the company on 30 August 2025 and holds no current role there. American authorities have been investigating Megaspeed since 2024 over concerns that it smuggled Nvidia's advanced artificial intelligence chips to China, and officials are still working to determine the full extent and duration of the pair's work with Chinese intelligence.

What the new reporting does not do is settle the central question. Trump administration officials have repeatedly said they have not concluded that Alice Huang spied for China, and that position was restated on Sunday. Attorney General Todd Blanche said this month that the Justice Department had not yet reached a conclusion on whether she was a Chinese spy, and the director of national intelligence, Jay Clayton, repeated that on CNN's "State of the Union" programme. "Attorney General Blanche has been very clear that this is a matter under investigation, both Ms Huang and her company, for various matters," Clayton said. "And I'm going to let that investigation play out." As [Reuters reported](https://www.reuters.com/technology/alice-huang-touch-with-chinese-spy-agency-during-affair-with-nvidia-ceo-nyt-says-2026-11-23/), American officials had already cast doubt last month on the initial suggestions that Huang was a spy, even as the new details show how sustained her contacts with the Ministry of State Security were.

The affair itself came to light on 29 October, when The New York Times reported that Huang had been identified by the United States as a Chinese intelligence asset and that Jensen Huang had been picked up on electronic surveillance targeting her. He acknowledged the affair only after that report, having first described his relationship with her as normal dealings with a business customer. The scandal led to his resignation as Nvidia's chief executive two weeks later and a steep fall in the company's share price. The Times had previously reported that Alice Huang and her family have a web of connections to Chinese defence contractors, and the latest report adds that she also appeared to have met officials from China's Ministry of Public Security, the country's main law enforcement agency.

The new details also raise questions about what the White House knew, and when. Advisers to President Donald Trump told him on at least two occasions that American intelligence had uncovered Huang's links to the Chinese spy agency and her relationship with Jensen Huang while he was still leading Nvidia, according to the report. Trump played down the concerns and indicated that he did not want to intervene, American officials cited by the newspaper said. Matt Pottinger, who served as deputy national security adviser during Trump's first term, told the Times that the network of companies involved in procuring and allegedly smuggling the chips aligned with the Ministry of State Security's stated objective of circumventing American export controls on semiconductors and other key technologies. The ministry has made acquiring high-end chips and advancing China's artificial intelligence ambitions a priority.

The scandal has prompted a broader reckoning in Washington over how tightly the United States polices its most prized semiconductors. Lawmakers from both parties have questioned whether the Trump administration has been too lax on the enforcement and regulation of advanced chips, and the affair has become the sharpest test yet of the export-control regime. Senator John Kennedy, a Louisiana Republican, told NBC's "Meet the Press" on Sunday that the affair itself was of less interest than the security questions around it. "I hope he had a good time," Kennedy said. "It was the most expensive sex since Helen of Troy." The episode has already shaken Nvidia itself: the company is under separate scrutiny from regulators, as covered in our report on the [SEC probe into Nvidia's accounting](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/sec-probes-nvidia-accounting-shares-plunge-november-2026), and it has since halted shipments of its H200 chips to China, detailed in our report on the [H200 halt](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/nvidia-halts-h200-chip-shipments-china-november-2026).

For now, the investigation continues on two tracks: the Justice Department's inquiry into Huang and Megaspeed, and the separate question of how many advanced chips reached China through the network of South-East Asian companies. No conclusion has been announced on either. Nvidia, Jensen Huang and the Chinese Embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to requests for comment, and Reuters said it had not been able to reach Alice Huang. The photograph with this article shows Jensen Huang delivering Nvidia's keynote at the CES technology show in Las Vegas in January 2025, not Alice Huang.
summary: The New York Times reports Alice Huang stayed in contact with an officer of China's Ministry of State Security from spring 2025 to autumn 2026, during her affair with former Nvidia chief Jensen Huang and while her firm Megaspeed bought large quantities of advanced Nvidia chips, some suspected of being smuggled to China — though US officials stress they have not concluded she spied.
title: US tracked Alice Huang's contacts with China's spy agency during Nvidia affair, NYT reports
